I am a GNU/Linux user and software developer, and I occasionally deal with networking and server administration.

I think this game is brilliant. It strikes a good balance between realism and fun, and those familiar with a Unix command line will feel right at home. At your disposal you have toy versions of real tools like nmap and scp, as well as some fictional cracking programs.

Your arsenal of tools grows as you roam the Internet and come across various handy .exe files that are circulated in the hacker communities. You can wreak havoc in (or just get information from) the filesystems of devices you have compromised. You can scan the network of a compromised device in order find more network nodes. You can set up a botnet of compromised devices. You can get hacked yourself. You can [spoiler]change the UI theme by switching out a file on your computer[/spoiler]. You can even open and close your optical drive!

All of this sets the stage for a very nice story in which you get to do some really crazy stuff.

If you have any kind of hacking knowledge you'll quickly realize that this and real world hacking can't be compared at all. That doesn't mean that it's a bad game though. It's a very nice typing puzzle game with a good story. Commands are fairly easy and you'll learn them fast. The quests/puzzles aren't too hard and always fair.

I’m not entirely sure what to think about this game. I feel like this game had the potential to be a lot more interesting than it turned out to be. I did have fun with this game and thought some of the missions were interesting. But, I can’t really figure out what this game is trying to be and I came away with the feeling that this game isn’t really finished. 

In terms of hacking and the operating system, it’s fairly weak and, at times, frustrating. The hacking programs you run are basically magic in terms of how powerful they are. They work on anything and require no modification based on the target. The challenge comes from managing your bizarre computer’s memory system and timing attacks to avoid the hollywood-style ‘tracing’. The simplified hacking mechanics aren’t a bad thing, I think. Real hacking elements would make the game extremely complicated, tedious, and boring. 

But, that aside, there are weird limitations on what you can do and what exists in the world. The operating system commands you run are unix-based, but quickly get frustrating to use for anyone familiar with *nix command lines. Autocompletion and wildcards are inconsistent (‘rm *’ works but not ‘rm file_*’). There is no cp (copy), mkdir, rmdir, rsync, or recursion-supported operations. There isn’t even a text editor of any kind, opting for a bizarre ‘replace’ to replace strings in a given file. This just causes more frustration than anything as folders become cluttered and basic OS actions can't be done.

As for the world, hacking into servers and snooping around is fun… to a point. You can read other people’s emails, deface websites, and steal files, which is fun! Then you realize that most of the files you discover are copy-pasted bash.org quotes or filler files which you can’t do anything with. Also, you’re strongly told early on to remove the log files you leave behind when hacking a server, but I’ve yet to find an instance where there are any consequences for not doing so outside of one mission. Finally, and probably my biggest problem, is that you’re pretty much the only active user on the entire internet. You’ll never accidentally encounter another hacker when breaking into a server and you’ll (with one exception) never find log files or evidence of dynamic activity from anyone else on the internet. The world is completely static, apart from a few scripted events. Maybe if there were random encounters or events with other hackers where both of you have the ability to hack each other and other servers, the world wouldn’t feel so static and empty and it would keep you on your toes a bit more. 

The investigation and puzzle aspects of the game are interesting. But, the large number of typos,  grammar mistakes (not sure if these two are intentional or not), and questionable writing can be distracting and confusing. That said, I still had fun. There are times where the missions can be very interesting and even disturbing. And, occasionally, there are times where you have to be clever to solve a puzzle or find a missing piece of information. But, those events are far and few in between. Most of the ‘contracts’ start to feel tedious pretty quickly.

Hacknet was an experience like no other. Its unique gameplay, tense moments and solid storyline got me hooked the moment I got that first message from Bit.

As an introduction to hacking, it does its job, but nothing more. I wouldn't expect anyone to be able to hack the Pentagon after playing this game. However, that does not detract one bit from the overall experience. It has a solid difficulty curve, so even the most computer-illiterate people will not have too much trouble. It is intuitive, and most importantly it is fun. Base game Hacknet provides an amazing 8 hour experience that everyone should check out. Not to mention the soundtrack, which is phenomenal.

With the Labyrinths DLC, Hacknet gets even more content in the form of a new storyline, new programs, new music and new puzzles. There is not much else to say then, the quality is the same, arguably better in the DLC, and I would recommend purchasing the DLC along with the base game.

Finally, there is a reason why I have so many hours in this game. Despite how amazing it is, Hacknet's story is somewhat short being 8 hours long, plus the DLC taking it to around 12 hours. I have played through the entire game plus DLC multiple times, but those never would have taken me to 100+ hours of playtime. No, I'm talking about mod support for the game, Hacknet Extensions. Extensions allows people to create their own storylines, puzzles, campaigns, etc. for other people to play. There are already many extensions to play, and as an active extensions developer myself, I can definitely say they add to the replayability of the game.

This game is really good. It's a pretty engaging hacking sim that has you using a terminal for most functions in the game. Very few things in this game do you actually use a mouse for. This isn't hollowood style "click on this and it'll magically take control of the world." It isn't a "real" hack simulation either. What is it then? Kinda like the fisher-price version of a real life linux terminal. You use real life commands on a terminal in this game, with watered down versions of real life port work on servers. No, it won't teach you how to be an 3L1t3 HAX0R, but it will engage you enough to probably inspire you to go out in the real world and learn about programming and what real hacking is. Might even inspire you to enter into a CTF competition online, where you can legally practice hacking skills in real competitions with varying difficulty, which is what I did after running through this game and getting inspired to learn more about programming and real-world hacking. If you hate typing a lot, you'll probably hate this game. It's not a bad thing, it's just how this game is played. But otherwise, if you're looking for a casual hack sim, nothing beats hacknet. The story is okay, but simply doing contracts that feel realistic and are very engaging and immersive is, imo, where the game shines. I also believe on 3/31/17 there is an expansion coming out that will add an addtional 3-4 hours of single player, as well as a multiplayer function where you work as a team to solve contracts or something (Don't quote me on that). If you take the time to dig through other networks in the game, a lot of the files will make you laugh from time to time.

TL;DR: Very fun, realistic-ish hacking simulator. Certainly more than worth its price, but don't get it if you despise typing. Also, some files in the game are kinda funny.

This was an incredible experience and definitely worth the money. A lot of games that attempt to be that Uplink successor are either very basic (read: butt ugly and short, with little to actually do) or are ridiculously complex and not very fun. This meets perfectly in the middle; easy to get into, giving you a lot of tools to work with that you have to use at the right times, while offering a fair and surmountable challenge. I do wish the act of "covering your tracks" were a bit more fleshed out, as in the game currently, all it entails is typing a quick command to delete everything in a "log" folder, but besides that, I never felt like the game was playing itself. I did in fact mess up a few times and and got one gameover while playing, so it definitely wasn't a breeze. 

The story itself was something of a page-turner; the characters felt real (given that your communications with people are through gramatically incorrect text interactions) and I felt genuine emotions towards and from the various characters you meet. Another small complaint was, when it was obvious that you were supposed to move on to a different "stage" of a game (i.e. wrap up the missions with one faction and go to the next one), that old faction more or less froze like a statue, their website never changed after that, and those characters (for the most part) were never seen nor heard from again. A bit of closure in that department would have been nice.

Anyway, very fun, not-too-long game, I'd but it again if I went back. Recommend for sure

Hacknet is a pretty entertaining hacking game for those that have an interest to stay long enough or of the genre.

To start, hacknet has a nice flow of events. The story is rather compelling and starts off fast. You are literally thrown into the events right away. The hacking is also somewhat similar to how the events would go in real life (to a degree of course) as some of this stuff is also what real life hackers employ from what I know. There are also interesting and funny parts of this game. At a certain point I remember hacking into a certain system and reading the logs. One of the logs was the top searched terms, and they were all like "Boobs" "Big Boobs" and stuff like that. The music for this game is also pretty good and fitting.

There are bad parts of this game as well. The biggest bad part is when you get hacked and are thrown into a screen without any directions to do anything. I was so confused at that point that I had to look at a guide to know what the hell was going on. Another bad part of this game is that its hard to get back into if you stop playing, as in it's hard to pick back up since some of the things are rather specific and easy to forget if you drop it for some time. Additionally, the game starts off really fast and you will be confused for a bit with all the different commands. I don't know how many times I had to bring up the help and notes. The game really doesn't have a particularly good transition from tutorial to game mode as well. Although you get to practice it a lot because there are a ton of hacking missions.

Overall, pretty good hacking game, but it is more meant for those interested in this genre.

Rating: 7.8/10
Recommend Price: $2.49 or lower.

I bought this game not really knowing what to expect of it but it seemed interesting enough to pick up on a sale.
It's definitely one of the most unique games I have ever played.
I assume that some people won't really enjoy this game because of the gameplay mechanics, the amount of reading and lack of visual content, but I highly enjoyed it.
In case you are worried about it being complicated due to the use of UNIX commands as the main playing tool, I can assure you that there is no reason for that.
I had absolutely 0 prior knowledge of any commands, but the game explains it in an easy to follow way and it doesn't take long to figure it out and get used to it. If you forget commands again, after a longer pause of not playing the game for example, you can always type in help and get a list of the most essential commands again.
While definitely an unusual gameplay mechanic it serves this game really well, as it makes you feel like a "real hacker", typing away on your keyboard and cracking those firewalls and proxys and ports and... 
The story is interesting and captivating as well and on top of that there are a lot of funny things hidden on the computers you're hacking. It's definitely worth looking around a little bit instead of just focusing on finding the information needed to progress in the main story.

So summed up, a very unique and enjoyable game, but probably not for everyone.
